source.title: Sparse Autoencoder Decomposition of Clinical Sequence Model Representations: Feature Complexity, Task Specialisation, and Mortality Prediction
source.authors: Chris Sainsbury; Feng Dong; Andreas Karwath

page_placements.theme: Feature abstraction grows with depth and over pretraining

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes SAE feature complexity across transformer layers, not across dictionary sizes. It does not test whether larger dictionaries split smaller-dictionary features into related features that partition their inputs.
record.gate_note: The study uses fixed 8×-expansion, 3,072-feature dictionaries for its main analysis and varies transformer layer, not dictionary size. It reports no parent–child feature matching, input partitioning, or geometric proximity across dictionary sizes. Mortality prediction and feature-perturbation results do not test the stated splitting claim and are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study trains TopK SAEs on a clinical EHR sequence model and measures feature complexity across transformer depth, cross-seed reproducibility, and downstream probe performance. Its one dictionary-size sweep (expansion 4, 8, 16 in Supp. Table S3) reports only explained variance and mortality AUC. It does not match features across dictionary sizes, so it neither tests splitting nor any version of it. SAEs are used as a tool and the study reports its own pipeline's performance, so the best fit is T4/uses_without_test rather than 'discusses', since splitting is never mentioned.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as far as it goes. The authors also conclude that, under full-sequence linear probes, SAE features beat dense representations for mortality but lose for length of stay. At leakage-safe windows, dense representations match or exceed SAE features. Delta-mode intervention cuts perturbation noise about 86×, but the perturbation effects are not significant.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains TopK SAEs on clinical sequence-model activations and measures feature properties across transformer layers. It does not perform the dictionary-size comparison needed to test splitting.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature-complexity measures vary with transformer layer; cross-seed feature matching also declines with depth. The study reports K-sensitivity for reconstruction and downstream task metrics, not for feature splitting.

fits_no_version.finding: INSPECT SAE features grow more complex with depth: singleton features fall from 45.7% to 0.5% and mean tokens per feature rise from 2.9 to 29.9 (layer 0 to layer 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this clinical sequence model, deeper-layer SAE features span more token types and clinical categories.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-seed decoder matching at cosine 0.7 falls from 42.3% at layer 0 to 19.8% at layer 9.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature reproducibility across seeds decreases with transformer depth in this model.

record.code_released: https://github.com/csainsbury/ascend-flat (currently private; contact the corresponding author for collaborator access)
record.problems: Only one 14.5-million-parameter model is studied. Individual feature identities have low cross-seed reproducibility, and the authors say downstream seed-wise variability was not formally quantified. The study does not compare dictionary sizes for the claim at issue.
record.rows_left_out: Mortality prediction, length-of-stay prediction, explained-variance sweeps, perturbation experiments, and feature case studies were omitted because they do not measure dictionary-size splitting or its defining relations.

untested.parts: No feature matching across dictionary sizes; the expansion sweep reports only EV and mortality AUC.
No splitting analysis in any model or open SAE release.
No nested feature families, geometry, or concept-hierarchy analysis.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, and no count of novel latents.
No test of the SAE objective's role in splitting and no Matryoshka comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from discusses/T6 to uses_without_test/T4: the paper applies SAEs as a tool and never mentions splitting. Supp. Table S3 varies expansion (4/8/16, i.e. 1,536 to 6,144 features) but reports only EV and mortality AUC. It does no feature-level comparison, so it does not bear on V1 or V5. Rows are accurately transcribed from Table 2 and Supp. Table S5; all are correctly linked to none.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of increasing dictionary sizes or tests of whether smaller features split into larger-dictionary features covering similar inputs and directions.
No dictionary-size splitting test across large models or open SAE releases.
No test of nested feature families, their geometric closeness, or whether they mirror a concept hierarchy.
No test of parent–child feature absorption or whether sparsity or dictionary size resolves it.
No decomposition comparison between larger- and smaller-dictionary latents, or test for novel latents across dictionary sizes.
No test of whether splitting is caused by the SAE objective or whether Matryoshka SAEs change it.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The text never mentions feature splitting. It cites Bricken et al. 2023 (and Templeton et al. 2024) only for SAE methodology and dead-feature resampling. It does not discuss or rely on the splitting finding.

tranche.reason: The study uses SAEs as its analysis method but never uses or tests the feature-splitting finding. It measures feature complexity across layers. Its only expansion sweep (Supp. Table S3) reports EV, mortality AUC and feature counts, with no splitting measure.

source_check.notes: Rows and statement match Table 2: FlatASCEND (14.5M) INSPECT SAEs, TopK 8x, K=16, layers 0 vs 6. This depth trend is not a dictionary-size splitting result. The expansion sweep (4/8/16 at INSPECT layer 6, Supp. Table S3) reports only EV, mortality AUC and feature count.
